introduction_markdown:
**Cameroon General Certificate of Education Board - General Certificate of Education Examination. Geography 2 (0750), Paper 2, ADVANCED LEVEL, JUNE 2022. Duration: THREE HOURS.**

Instructions to candidates: Answer FOUR questions, choosing at least ONE from each Section.

Each question carries twenty-five marks. You are encouraged to refer to specific examples drawn from any part of the world. Credit will be given for such specific examples.

Only the required number of questions will be marked.

Marks will be awarded for well annotated maps and diagrams where these are relevant.

You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers.

questions.enonce_markdown:
a) Examine any **THREE** reasons why government intervenes in the agricultural sector.

(9 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
Agriculture is the main activity of the rural population in most countries and it is a sector in which the market alone often gives poor results. **Governments intervene** (by subsidies, guaranteed prices, credit, research and extension, land reform, marketing boards and state-owned agro-industrial companies) for many reasons. Three are examined here (3 marks each).

1. **To ensure food security and reduce food imports.** A government must feed the population and does not want to depend on imports, which cost foreign currency and expose the country to world price rises and shortages. It therefore helps farmers increase food production by supplying subsidised fertilisers, improved seeds and credit, by irrigation (for example the rice schemes of the Yagoua area of northern Cameroon run by the state company SEMRY) and by extension services and research.
2. **To stabilise and raise farmers' incomes and prices.** Farm output varies from year to year with the weather, perishable products must be sold quickly and the demand for food is inelastic, so prices and incomes fluctuate. Governments fix guaranteed minimum prices, buy surpluses or give subsidies (as under the Common Agricultural Policy of the European Union) to protect farmers from poverty, keep them on the land and reduce rural-urban migration. In Cameroon, state support has long been given to the organisation and marketing of crops such as cotton (SODECOTON), cocoa and coffee.
3. **To earn foreign exchange and supply raw materials to industry.** Export crops such as cocoa, coffee, cotton, bananas, rubber and palm oil bring in foreign currency, and they supply agro-industries (textile mills, vegetable-oil mills, sugar factories). The state encourages their production by plantation schemes (such as those of the Cameroon Development Corporation, CDC), subsidies, marketing arrangements and infrastructure.

*Other reasons:* to promote **regional development** and equality between rural and urban areas, to settle the landless through land reform, to **protect the environment** and soils (soil conservation, anti-desertification measures, limits on the use of chemicals), to introduce **modern technology**, and to provide infrastructure (feeder roads, storage and markets) that individual farmers cannot afford.

**Conclusion.** State intervention is justified by the strategic importance of food and the risks of farming, although it may lead to waste, corruption and dependence on subsidies when badly managed.

questions.enonce_markdown:
b) Briefly explain the following terms:

i) Industrial Inertia.

ii) Location Quotient.

iii) Industrial Agglomeration.

(10 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Industrial inertia** is the **tendency of an industry to remain in its original location even after the factors that first attracted it (raw materials, a source of power, a local market) have lost their importance or disappeared**. The industry stays because of the large capital already invested in factories and machinery, the pool of skilled labour, the existing transport and services, the links with other firms, and the reputation of the place. Examples are the steel and engineering industries of Sheffield and Birmingham in England, which remained long after the local coal and iron ore had been exhausted or become uneconomic.

**(ii) Location quotient (LQ)** is a **statistical index of the degree of concentration of an industry in a region compared with the nation**:

$$
LQ = \frac{e_i / e}{E_i / E}
$$

where $e_i$ is the employment in industry i in the region, $e$ the total employment in the region, $E_i$ the national employment in industry i and $E$ the total national employment. An LQ greater than 1 shows that the industry is more concentrated in the region than in the country as a whole (the region is specialised in it); an LQ equal to 1 means it has the same share as in the whole country; an LQ below 1 means under-representation. For example, if textiles employ 20% of the workers of a region and 10% of the workers of the country, $LQ = 20/10 = 2.0$.

**(iii) Industrial agglomeration** is the **clustering of many industrial firms (often related firms) in the same place**, to take advantage of **agglomeration economies**: a common pool of skilled labour, shared infrastructure (roads, port, power, water), specialised suppliers and services, links between firms (one firm's product is another's raw material), ready markets, and the finance and information available in the area. Examples are the Ruhr in Germany, Silicon Valley in California and, in Cameroon, the industrial zones of Douala. Growth is limited when congestion, high land costs and pollution produce diseconomies.

questions.enonce_markdown:
c) Analyse any **TWO** indices used in measuring transport network connectivity.

(6 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
A transport network is represented as a **graph** of **nodes (vertices, v)** such as towns or ports, joined by **links (edges, e)** such as roads or railways. **Connectivity** measures how well the nodes are linked. Two of the indices (3 marks each) are analysed here, with a worked example for a network of 6 towns joined by 7 roads (v = 6, e = 7).

**1. Beta index (β)** compares the number of links with the number of nodes.

$$
\beta = \frac{e}{v} = \frac{7}{6} = 1.17
$$

- A **tree** network (no circuits) has $\beta < 1$ (e.g. v - 1 links give $\beta$ below 1); $\beta = 1$ means a single circuit; **$\beta > 1$** means that there are several circuits, hence a more complex and better connected network. A value of 1.17 shows a network with a few alternative routes. The index is simple, but it does not have a fixed upper limit, so it is not easy to compare networks of very different sizes.

**2. Gamma index (γ)** is the ratio of the number of links observed to the **maximum number possible** for the same number of nodes (for a planar network, $3(v - 2)$).

$$
\gamma = \frac{e}{3\,(v - 2)} = \frac{7}{3 \times 4} = 0.58
$$

- The value lies between **0 (no links) and 1 (every possible link present, 100% connected)**; here the network has 58% of the possible links, so it is moderately connected. It is easy to compare different networks, but it does not describe the pattern of the links.

**Other indices:** the **alpha index** $\alpha = \dfrac{e - v + 1}{2v - 5} = \dfrac{2}{7} = 0.29$ (the number of circuits as a proportion of the maximum possible), the **cyclomatic number** $\mu = e - v + 1 = 2$ (the number of independent circuits) and the **detour index** (actual route distance divided by straight-line distance, multiplied by 100, which measures the directness of a route).

**Conclusion.** The higher the values of β and γ, the better connected the network, which indicates greater accessibility, more alternative routes and usually a more developed region (the dense road networks of southern Cameroon and of Europe contrast with the sparse networks of the North and East of Cameroon).
